item.title: A Bank Instead of the Dollar: Why Iran Is Racing to Join BRICS's Development Bank Mid-War
item.body:
## A Financial Lifeline Sought Amid Conflict

Even as fighting with the United States and Israel remains unresolved and sanctions continue to squeeze its economy, Iran is pushing hard on a different front: banking diplomacy. Officials at Iran's central bank have said in recent statements that the country's long-pursued membership in the BRICS New Development Bank (NDB) is nearing completion — a move that, if finalized, would give Tehran access to project financing and payment channels that operate outside the U.S. dollar system.

The timing is notable. Most countries pursue multilateral financial memberships during periods of relative stability, when technical and legal groundwork can proceed without geopolitical noise. Iran is instead advancing this bid in the middle of active hostilities, which underscores just how central "de-dollarization" has become to its economic survival strategy.

## What the New Development Bank Actually Is

Founded in 2015 by Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa — the original BRICS members — the New Development Bank was designed as an alternative to Western-led institutions like the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund. It funds infrastructure and sustainable development projects, and increasingly issues loans in local currencies rather than U.S. dollars, a feature that has made it attractive to countries seeking to reduce their exposure to dollar-based sanctions.

Iran formally joined the broader BRICS group as a full member in January 2024, alongside Egypt, Ethiopia and the United Arab Emirates. Membership in BRICS itself, however, is separate from membership in the NDB, which has its own governance process, capital contribution requirements and voting structure. Iranian officials have periodically signaled progress on this second, more technical step, framing it as a natural extension of BRICS accession rather than a new initiative.

## Why a Bank Matters More Than a Bloc

For a country under some of the most extensive sanctions regimes in the world, symbolic bloc membership only goes so far. What Iran needs, according to economists who track sanctioned economies, is actual liquidity: financing for infrastructure, energy and trade projects that Western-aligned banks and institutions are barred — or unwilling — to provide.

NDB membership would theoretically open a channel for exactly that. It would also allow Iran to settle at least some transactions with fellow member states in currencies other than the dollar, reducing the risk that payments get frozen or blocked as they pass through the dollar-clearing system, where U.S. regulators have significant oversight.

Analysts caution, however, that the practical impact should not be overstated. The NDB's total lending capacity is a fraction of that of the World Bank, and the bank itself must weigh how closely it wants to associate with a heavily sanctioned member, given its own need to raise capital in international markets where Western investors remain important. Russia's experience — a founding NDB member that has faced difficulty accessing the bank's own resources since 2022 due to compliance concerns among other shareholders — is often cited as a cautionary example.

## A Broader Pattern, Not an Isolated Case

Iran's push fits into a wider trend among sanctioned or sanctions-wary economies to build financial infrastructure that sits outside traditional Western oversight. Russia, China and several Gulf states have all, in different ways, expanded local-currency trade agreements, alternative payment messaging systems, and non-dollar reserve holdings over the past several years.

Whether this amounts to a genuine structural shift away from dollar dominance — or simply a set of workarounds for a small number of heavily sanctioned states — remains a subject of debate among economists. The dollar still accounts for the large majority of global trade invoicing and central bank reserves, and institutions like the NDB remain small by comparison.

## What to Watch Next

The key markers going forward are procedural rather than dramatic: whether Iran's NDB accession is formally ratified by the bank's board, what capital contribution and voting share it is assigned, and how quickly — if at all — the bank moves to approve project financing for Iranian initiatives. Given the bank's cautious posture toward existing sanctioned members, most observers expect any tangible financial benefit to Iran to be gradual rather than immediate, even after formal membership is confirmed.

For now, the story is less about an imminent alternative to the dollar and more about how sanctioned states are quietly building the scaffolding for one, one institutional membership at a time.
